profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a mid-sized SaaS company that has multiple internal teams building prompt-enabled features, including a customer-support copilot and a knowledge assistant. The company is considering an internal 'promptware engineering workbench' and needs a credible MVP story for an upcoming architecture review. The agenda is to generate and narrow down candidate features that would make prompt development less ad hoc, especially around versioning, testing, and team workflows. The expected outcome is a short list of 2-3 MVP feature themes that both participants believe can anchor the proposal for next quarter.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: LLM infrastructure, evaluation pipelines, developer tooling, observability
members.background: Priya leads platform work for the company's model-serving and experimentation stack and previously built CI/CD systems for ML services before moving into LLM applications.
members.private_state: She wants the proposal to reuse existing engineering workflows and avoid committing the platform team to a large bespoke product surface that would be expensive to maintain.
hidden_assumptions: When people say a 'prompt' should be versioned, the practical artifact is mainly the system instruction text plus variable placeholders, while tool schemas, retrieval settings, and response parsers remain separate code artifacts.
A 'representative regression set' should be traffic-shaped and drawn from recent production traces, because that is the most realistic way to catch regressions without hand-curating scenarios.
For probabilistic LLM systems, 'CI integration' should mostly mean deterministic linting at PR time and heavier model-based checks in nightly or scheduled jobs rather than blocking merges.
The default users of any prompt tooling are engineers already comfortable with Git, YAML, and pull-request review, so collaboration features can be minimal in an MVP.

members.name: Daniel Wu
members.role: Senior Product Manager, AI Developer Experience
members.expertise: Internal platform strategy, workflow design, adoption of developer tools, cross-functional product operations
members.background: Daniel owns internal AI tooling adoption across product teams and previously launched low-code workflow tools used by PMs, analysts, and support-ops specialists as well as engineers.
members.private_state: He wants the MVP to feel broadly useful and demoable across teams, especially to non-platform stakeholders, so the architecture review will fund a larger initiative.
hidden_assumptions: When teams talk about a 'prompt' artifact, they mean the full prompt package that shapes model behavior, including instructions, few-shot examples, tool descriptions, output format guidance, and related notes.

A 'representative regression set' should be a compact curated suite of canonical scenarios spanning user journeys and risk categories, because stakeholders need visible coverage rather than traffic realism alone.
If something is 'in CI,' teams will expect pre-merge pass/fail feedback attached to the pull request; otherwise it will not change behavior or feel like a real engineering control.
Prompt authors are not just engineers but also PMs, support-ops specialists, and policy reviewers, so an MVP should assume browser-based collaboration and lightweight approval workflows.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the prompt artifact
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'versioning the prompt' or a 'prompt package' as if it names the same artifact.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means versioning the core prompt text and its variables, with other behavior-shaping assets handled elsewhere in code or config.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means versioning the full behavior package around the model call, including prompt text, examples, tool instructions, output guidance, and related context.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In LLM work, people often use 'prompt' loosely to refer either to the raw instruction text or to the entire assembled interaction spec, so the phrase sounds naturally aligned in a brainstorming meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes a regression set representative
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse building a 'representative regression set' for comparing prompt changes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes representative means a statistically realistic sample of recent production traces, weighted by actual traffic patterns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes representative means a deliberately curated set of canonical cases covering major workflows, edge cases, and risk categories.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are professionally defensible and both fit the word 'representative,' so neither participant hears anything strange unless the sampling method is explicitly unpacked.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that evaluation should be 'wired into CI.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes CI means PR-time static checks plus scheduled model evaluations run nightly or asynchronously because live LLM checks are costly and noisy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes CI means pre-merge automated model evaluations that produce a visible pass/fail signal on the pull request.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software engineering, 'CI' routinely suggests automated validation around code changes, but LLM teams quietly vary on whether expensive probabilistic checks are blocking or scheduled, making the mismatch easy to miss.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about helping 'authors' and improving the 'review workflow' without defining the user group.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the authors are engineers editing prompt files in repos and reviewing changes through standard pull requests.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes authors include non-engineering contributors who need a shared UI, comments, and approvals outside a pure code workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants work with real prompt contributors in their own circles, so each treats their user picture as obvious background context rather than a point needing clarification.

turns.inner_thought: We need something credible for the architecture review that doesn't sign my team up for building a giant standalone prompt product. If we can frame this as extensions to existing repo workflows, eval pipelines, and observability, it stays in-bounds. Support copilot is the best anchor because they already have traces and prompt churn, and the knowledge assistant can be a second example.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The architecture review is coming up fast, and we need a tight MVP story for a promptware engineering workbench—something concrete enough that the support copilot teams can immediately see the value. My goal today is to get to a short list of maybe two or three feature themes we can stand behind for next quarter.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to sound bigger than a niche platform utility for infra-minded engineers. If the story is about making prompt changes safer and easier for authors across functions, it becomes fundable. I want reviewers imagining PMs, ops, and policy folks using it too, not just engineers editing files.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I think the framing should be: how do we make prompt changes safer and easier for authors across teams, so prompt development doesn't feel like trial-and-error with no guardrails? If we can show a better review workflow and more confidence in changes, that's a pretty compelling narrative.

turns.inner_thought: Start with the lowest-risk, highest-leverage piece: version the prompt in the repo, give teams diffs, history, and rollback, and keep everything in normal engineering workflows. In my head that's the system prompt text and variables as a first-class artifact, not every surrounding config object. That keeps scope manageable and maintainable.
turns.utterance: Yeah. One core theme could just be versioning the prompt in the repo with clean diffs, history, and rollback. A lot of teams are still changing things in scattered places, and if we let them treat prompt updates more like code changes, we already remove a lot of the ad hoc pain.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but for this to resonate broadly, 'the prompt' has to feel like the whole thing someone is reviewing, not just a slice of text. I want a reviewer to open one artifact and understand behavior, examples, guidance, and context. Also, review workflow can't assume everyone lives in Git all day.
turns.utterance: I like that. And I think the prompt package should be rich enough that, when someone opens it, they can understand what they're reviewing in one place—examples, tool instructions, relevant context, that sort of thing. That would make the review workflow much clearer for authors and stakeholders.

turns.inner_thought: Next theme: regression evaluation, but grounded in reality. The best representative regression set is traffic-shaped from recent support traces; otherwise people hand-pick a showcase suite that misses real regressions. We can anonymize and sample production conversations, then compare prompt versions automatically.
turns.utterance: A second theme could be evaluation around a representative regression set, so teams can compare prompt versions without manually replaying everything. For the support use case especially, we have enough recent traces that this could become a practical baseline instead of one-off spot checks.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and that set needs to visibly cover the journeys leadership cares about. If reviewers can point to onboarding, billing, escalations, policy-sensitive moments, they will believe the system is protecting against real product risk. I don't need a giant dataset; I need legible coverage.
turns.utterance: Agreed. If we do that, the representative regression set should give people confidence that the important cases are covered—onboarding, billing, escalations, sensitive policy edge cases, the places where teams really want to know a change is safe. That makes the evaluation story easier to trust.

turns.inner_thought: I need to steer CI toward something operationally sane: linting and schema checks on every PR, then heavier model-based comparisons asynchronously or on a schedule. Blocking merges on noisy LLM evals will create pain and we'll own the fallout. 'Wired into CI' is still true if the expensive checks run nightly and feed dashboards or alerts.
turns.utterance: Right, and I'd definitely want those checks wired into CI. At minimum we can run prompt linting and validation on every PR, then have the broader behavioral checks watching for drift over time so teams aren't flying blind after changes land.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—CI is exactly where I want the signal. But for adoption, teams need pass/fail on the PR itself or they won't treat it as real governance. If a prompt change just disappears into some later dashboard, behavior won't change. Also, that visible review loop is important for non-engineering authors.
turns.utterance: Yes—if evaluation is wired into CI and teams get pass/fail results attached to the PR, it starts to feel like a real control instead of a side report. That also makes prompt changes look much more reviewable, which helps the overall workflow for authors.

turns.inner_thought: We probably need some kind of editor, but I want it lightweight and close to the repo, not a whole new collaborative app. Maybe a simple playground that lets engineers compare revisions, run a few test cases, and then open a PR. Keep the product surface small; reuse existing auth, repos, and deployment paths.
turns.utterance: The last area I'd put on the table is a lightweight editor or playground that sits close to the repo. Something where authors can compare prompt revisions side by side, try changes quickly, and then move into review without a bunch of copy-paste between tools.

turns.inner_thought: This is shaping up well. I can package it as versioning, evaluation, and collaborative authoring—a story that feels broad enough for multiple teams and visible enough to demo. In my head, the MVP should hint at browser-based collaboration and approvals, even if implementation starts narrower.
turns.utterance: I think that's a solid structure for the review. We can frame the MVP around three themes: versioning the prompt, a representative regression set with evaluation wired into CI, and a stronger collaborative authoring and review workflow. That gives us a narrative that's practical for the support copilot team but still clearly extensible across the other prompt-heavy teams.
